newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: U.S. seeks strong WTO declaration on agriculture.
newsitem.headline: U.S. seeks strong WTO declaration on agriculture.

text.p: The United States is seeking a strong statement on agricultural trade in the final conference declaration of trade ministers gathered in Singapore, Deputy U.S. Agriculture Secretary Richard Rominger said on Wednesday.

"The report from the committee on agriculture here re-affirms the Marrakesh schedules and also lays out the work agenda for the next two years and then the 1999 resumption of negotiations," Rominger told Reuters in an interview.
"We don't want countries going away from here thinking they can relax and think they can do nothing until 1999," he said.

Rominger was attending the first ministerial meeting of the World Trade Organization (WTO) being held in Singapore and which concludes on Friday. Agriculture was bought under the aegis of the WTO in Marrakesh at the conclusion of the Uruguay Round.

Rominger said the U.S. was pushing for the elimination of all agricultural subsidies in the next round of talks and was also focusing on sanitary and phytosanitary issues (SPS) and state trading enterprises (STEs).
He said although the Uruguay Round had made good progress on reducing tariffs, SPS issues and STEs had increasingly emerged as obstacles to trade over the past two years.

"We need some reform in the administration of tariff rate quotas, the elimination of unjustified SPS. We're seeing from the notifications that we're getting that not every country is living up to the reforms. We need to do some work on the STEs."
He identified the European Union states and Japan as countries wishing to slow the pace of agricultural reform.
Rominger said the U.S. had problems with the EU over health issues, but expected to win a WTO dispute panel ruling on hormones in beef exports next spring.
"The next big issue (with the EU) is the equivalency of our meat inspection systems which will have a big effect on our exports, the biggest section of which is pet food," he said.

He said the EU hadn't done the technical work to harmonise the acceptance of U.S. meat inspection systems with its own, because Brussels had introduced new restrictions due to concerns over mad cow disease which threatened serious disruption of trade.
The U.S. is also focusing on the role of state trading enterprises in agriculture particularly in Canada, Australia, New Zealand and China, Rominger added.
Rominger said that international trade agreements such as the WTO and NAFTA were working and the U.S. was enjoying record agricultural exports of $60 billion this year.
"Agriculture is one of the areas where we remain competitive and where we have a comparitive advantage.
We want to see that comparitive advantage recognised," said U.S. Department of Agriculture Foreign Agricultural Service administrator, August Schumacher.
"That is what the WTO is all about," he said.
Schumacher, who was accompanying Rominger, added that the U.S. would expect very strong agricultural trade reform proposals from China before it was accepted into the WTO.
He said Washington had problems with China on the transparency of its agricultural trade policies and SPS and STE issues.

"People don't realise that China is a major net food exporter with sales of $12 billion a year and is a major competitor for the U.S. in Asia in sectors such as poultry, fruit and vegetables," Schumacher said.
